Way back in 1964, when Murray Gell-Mann proposed the theory that protons and neutrons are actually made up of even tinier charged subatomic particles called quarks. There six types of quarks, and for every type, there is an anti-matter opposite called an antiquark. The theory also implied that even more complex quark structures of five, six, or even seven quarks could form larger particles. The actual term "pentaquark" wasn't coined however until 1987, by Harry Lipkin.

Pentaquarks were thought to have been observed in the years 2000, 2003, and 2008. They were finally, definitively observed in 2015 -believe it or not- by accident durring an experiment designed to observe matter-antimatter asymmetry.

Being able to study pentaquarks will do a few things. It will allow us to better understand the physics of neutron stars. It will also let physicists gain a deeper understanding of the strong force (you can learn more about that HERE) and Quantum chromodynamics (more about that HERE).

Zombioptic pretty much hit the nail on the head. The only thing I'll add is that the discovery of the pentaquark is analogous to finding new ways to combine legos that were previously theorized but not verified. We now know for sure that different particles can be formed in ways we had yet to observe.

So, I've been working on little things for the past couple of months (test websites and stuff) to advance my coding skills, and now I want to launch a full proper website.

The problem I've seen with a lot of reddit alternatives like slicer, commentum, etc, is that they're completely dead. Possibly because they aren't different enough to reddit/voat to warrant going there.

I saw a vid here posted a week or so back about how reddit built its community. Basically, the admins posted content under fake usernames to make it "look" alive. And that lit a lightbulb in my head. You could make a community "look" active if you used fake votes, fake comments/usernames to make it look alive and active. The only problem is that it'd take a lot of effort on your behalf to constantly come up with new submissions and comments (after all, you're the only one commenting for now).

Is this immoral? I am seriously considering doing this to get my website off the ground once I launch it.
How to successfully build a community?

One thing that you really need to take into consideration when you're building this website of yours is "What is it offering?"

What will it offer other people that Reddit or Voat don't already do.

A lot of people left reddit for voat because they were tired of the admins getting a little too power hungry and limiting the "Free speech" that they highlighted as a selling point in previous interviews.

How is your community going to differ from the other platforms like this? People won't just jump ship to your platform even with fresh content being posted, because the truth of the matter is that Reddit or Voat will always have the most up to date content.

Having said all that, what's your selling point?

Yep, this is something I've noticed from all the various reddit alternatives. They don't offer anything unique compared to Voat/reddit, or if they do, it's a tiny worthless gimmick that won't keep people around using it. Voat/reddit have the largest communities, so why would you go to the same thing, but way way smaller? (Well, you wouldn't.)

My goal is to offer some unique features (which I have thought of and trying to implement) as well as keep it updated with really interesting/unique content to start with.

The fake users are called sockpuppets and they are generally frowned on. The ethicality depends on their use. As far as just using sockpuppets to promote interesting content, like a books sockpuppet, a music sockpuppet, etc. I don't see anything unethical there.
